title: Beautiful Succession
author: Becky Abrams Wilmoth
summary: Becky Abrams Wilmoth, founder of a homeschool co-op that grew into a hybrid program with a second campus, writes about the underdiscussed problem of founder turnover in the fast-growing school-choice movement. Her core argument is that leaders and boards celebrate program creation and expansion but rarely plan for the moment a founder needs to step away, and that intentional succession planning, not heroic founder endurance, determines whether a program survives that transition. She traces her own accidental succession process: operational necessity forced her to document processes, policies, and procedures and train Campus Directors two years before she resigned, which meant the program didn't collapse when she left. The piece closes on an emotional register, comparing running a program to parenting: you pour your life into something so that eventually it can continue without you, and watching it thrive at a remove, even painfully, is described as its own kind of beauty.
points: Names founder and leader turnover as an underdiscussed risk in the fast-growing school-choice and homeschool-co-op movement, arguing infrastructure builders should plan for it rather than assume founder permanence.

Argues succession planning works best when driven by operational necessity well before a departure, since documenting processes and training successors two years ahead prevented the program's collapse when she resigned.
Calls for organizations like VELA and Herzog to expand support frameworks (free tools, funding, respite) for founders specifically so programs aren't structurally dependent on one person's endurance.
Frames succession as an act of humility comparable to parenting: building something so it can eventually function, and even flourish, entirely without its founder.
quotes: With this view in mind, we can and should anticipate something that is not discussed quite as often, turnover. Founders and leaders get tired. Priorities change. Personal and family needs change.
Support, encouragement, and respite for founders and leaders should be paramount to board members, parents, and other infrastructure builders in this ecosystem.

I spent the better part of two years documenting processes, policies, procedures, and training leaders to carry on the work that I had done. And when personal circumstances changed and I needed to step away, it wasn't devastating to the program.

The program that I (and a few others) worked so hard to build almost entirely from scratch has taken on a life of its own. The leaders and families involved now carry the torch and continue to move the mission forward.
Starting and running a successful program really isn't all that different from parenting. You pour your life into it, it nearly kills you, and then one day, it doesn't need you anymore.
